newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour sees huge poll lead eroded.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour sees huge poll lead eroded.

text.p: The British Labour Party's huge opinion poll lead dipped sharply after a week of election campaigning in which the ruling Conservatives claimed they were finally winning the argument against their main opponents.

Two polls in Sunday's newspapers gave Labour a 16-point lead over Prime Minister John Major's Conservative Party, down as much as seven points from a week ago, while a third poll said Labour had a 20-point lead, down four points.
Early in the campaign for the May 1 election, Labour, led by reformer Tony Blair, was ahead by up to 28 points in the polls and looked set for a landslide victory.

But the Conservatives, in what they termed a "wobbly week" for Labour, turned their fire on its traditional links with the trades unions and on Blair's statement that Labour would no longer rule out privatising some state assets.
They say Blair, while claiming to have shifted Labour to the centre ground, has persuaded the unions to remain in the background until after the election and then he will bow to their demands.

One Sunday newspaper report said Blair could face problems over relations with the unions later this week when, it said, representatives at the Scottish Trades Union Congress were expected to demand a series of concessions from Labour.

Major's deputy, Michael Heseltine, seized on the report. "The union dinosaurs who wrecked our economy throughout the 60s and 70s and who tried so hard to subvert our success in creating a vibrant enterprise economy in the 80s are on the march again," he said.

Blair denied that if he won power he would allow the unions, who make large contributions to Labour Party funds, to regain the sway they had over Britain in the 1970s and he would not give in to union calls for high pay settlements.

"No one has expectations that they will vote Labour on Thursday and the money will start rolling on Friday. People know that is not the case. I believe the unions understand that, if they don't they will find out," he told the Sunday Times.

Blair defended his apparent change of policy over privatising Britain's air traffic control services, saying he had to consider it because it would be part of the spending plans inherited from the Conservatives if Labour won power.
But another newspaper said members of Blair's shadow cabinet were angry over his change in tack on privatisation, especially because they had not been told about it in advance.
